Located in the city’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, the Monos office was created to reflect the brand’s development to date and provide space for continued growth. Ste Marie was presented with an open-ended brief, allowing the studio to develop a “flexible framework” for a company that is “still exploring what it could become” and would allow its team to collaborate, experiment and host. Photography Previous Next Photography Close “Monos is a brand grounded in design, mindfulness, human connection, and we understood this as an opportunity to create a place where those values could be put into practice,” said Ste Marie. “A place where their people could come together to work, create, exchange ideas, test new things, host events and gather as an extended community.” The studio, which previously designed the interiors for a Monos store in Toronto , approached the workplace like a residential project and organised the spaces into three overlapping areas. “Like an apartment, it accommodates everyday activity as naturally as moments of hosting,” said the studio. “The residential quality also supports Monos’ culture of openness.” The first area features low, soft modular sofas for lounging and conversation, and enclosed banquettes below conical pendant lights that facilitate personal exchanges, small meetings or shared meals. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Previous Next Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. “The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity,” Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. “The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language.” The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Located in Manchester , Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges. The design was informed by the founders’ experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound. “When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space,” Cossins told Dezeen. Bar Shrimp’s interior draws on mid-century bar decor The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics. Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo. The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials. DJs provide a curated music programme throughout the day “We’re looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective,” said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Danie

Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends. HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood. “We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of ‘dwelling’,” HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen. Terracotta red and earthy yellow are used as the main colours of this building The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis. However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site. The slab is 1.1 metres thick and sits 4.9 metres above the ground The hotel’s entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a “water curtain” that falls from surrounding walkway. Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat , the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as “pre-illness”. The hotel is the third project designed by Ban for Japanese company Pasona Group on the island. It follows a thatch-topped restaurant and a wooden meditation retreat . Shigeru Ban designed the Pasona Natureverse Retreat According to Ban, the hotel’s D-shaped form was designed to take advantage of its location between the coast and a forest. “To express the characteristics of a site defined by these two completely contrasting landscapes, distinct facades were designed for the east and west sides,” said Ban. “Two linear structures with individual qualities are integrated into a single D-shaped plan, flanking a light-filled atrium.” The hotel stands on the seafront The five-storey hotel was designed primarily for long-term, 30-day-plus retreats, as well as offering shorter stays. Its 57 rooms are arranged around a large, skylit central atrium with half overlooking the sea and half facing the forest. While the landward facade is adorned with stylised timber columns, the seaward side was designed to express horizontally, with balconies running the full width on all levels. KTGY ‘s Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level. KTGY has revamped the Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park hotel Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago’s Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it’s crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels. However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the “postmodern” descriptions of the building. The scope included lounges and premium rooms The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper’s facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale. “KTGY’s interiors team reflected the building’s postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale,” said the team. The Dean Munich is the latest offering from the Irish hotel chain , with 281 rooms and suites, three bars, and a signature Japanese restaurant named Ibasho. The design blends influences from art nouveau and 1980s nightclubs The project saw von Stein revamp an existing hotel in the city’s Westend neighbourhood, with a design where shades of gold and red extend across velvet furniture, floral carpets, stained-glass windows and ornamental lamps. The project allowed the interior designer to dig into the design history of the city where she was born. Her scheme blends the city’s distinct Jugendstil style, the manifestation of art nouveau in Bavaria, with the decadent nightclubs that proliferated in the 1980s. The lobby features a restored floor of black stone chevron tiles “This is a city rooted in history but always drawn to reinvention,” said von Stein. “I wanted to capture that tension, somewhere between elegance and exuberance, and let it guide every surface, object and gesture.” “The design also brings to life a side of Munich only locals truly know – its rich musical and cultural spirit, quietly woven into the character of the city.” On a raised platform, a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess The most radical interventions are in the communal areas on the gro

Occupying the basement levels of a building in Marylebone, Dive features furniture and materials that adapt to different scenarios and celebrate signs of use. Golem has designed the interiors for Marylebone bar Dive “Dive’s experience is an ongoing negotiation between the design and its guests,” explained Golem founder Ariel André. “The bar is not finished at opening, it is finished nightly, by hands, shoes, spills.” “Wear and tear is part of the architecture,” he added. “Glossy surfaces are designed to take scratches from glasses and jewellery, velvety walls and floors are meant to retain the imprint of bodies.” The bar is covered almost entirely in red velvet Dive’s owner chose to divide the venue into two distinct zones: a luminous bar area near the entrance and a darker, more intimate lounge reached by descending a short flight of steps. Clean lines and sculptural forms define the bar, which features a curved cutout along its front. Convex mirrors and surfaces rendered in smooth, glossy finishes reflect light and movement throughout the space. The fabric retains “the imprint of bodies” “The palette and shimmering light are calibrated for a transitional feel, somewhere between dusk and dawn: warm enough to flatter skin tones, restrained enough to leave the shimmering cocktails in focus,” André explained. When designer and artist Eva Gold was put in charge of the bar’s interiors, television and cinema ended up being key points of reference – fitting given that Hausu was named after a 1977 Japanese horror-comedy film. Located in Manchester , Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges. The design was informed by the founders’ experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound. “When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space,” Cossins told Dezeen. Bar Shrimp’s interior draws on mid-century bar decor The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics. Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo. The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials. DJs provide a curated music programme throughout the day “We’re looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective,” said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Danie

A London Couple Asked for “Edgy and Raw.” Max Radford Delivered. We’re gagging over this London townhouse, from the teal-and-steel bathroom to the vintage paintings in the dining room to how Italian classics meld perfectly with works by up-and-comers. Photos: Michael Sinclair In one of the best interior briefs I’ve heard, the clients of this late-Victorian home in London wanted something “edgy, contemporary, and a little bit raw” — the diametric opposite, basically, of the Pinterest aesthetic. They certainly came to the right person: Max Radford , who not only runs an eponymous gallery for new talents working under pretty much the same directives, but also designs interiors as such, often incorporating pieces from his roster. Likeminded clients are every designer’s dream, but the project has me thinking with pride about how far our little world has come. It’s hard to imagine clients with-it enough to hire a decorator this way 15, or even 10, years ago. Or if they did, to give them both carte blanche and a budget (rather than either/or). Working atop an existing renovation by Atomik Architecture, Radford came through in spectacular fashion, but took care not to abuse his mandate; he added in the requisite 20th-century icons like sofas by Pierre Paulin and Alessandro Becchi, lights by the Castiglionis and Mario Botta, and a bed by Carlo Scarpa before wilding out with more directional new British talents — and that scrumptious teal-walled bathroom. The living room features a zigzag steel chair by Grace Prince, the entry hall a custom radiator cover by Radford himself, the bedroom a cabinet by EJR Barnes, and the bathroom a chair by LS Gomma as well as a mirror by Radford and Eddie Olin. A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designe

Art and Architecture Find a Perfect Dialogue Inside a Modernist Connecticut Landmark Artworks made from paper layered on top of linen canvases by Kim Bartelt, on view through tomorrow at the 1960 John Landis–designed Gores Pavilion in Connecticut. One downside of taking an annual summer break from our newsletter: We sometimes miss the window for exhibitions and other time-sensitive projects. This site-specific exhibition of new work by Berlin artist Kim Bartelt is only on view until the end of the day tomorrow, but assuming most of you aren’t anywhere near New Canaan, Connecticut, anyway, we figured we might as well enable you to enjoy it from afar. For “Exhibit No. 2,” presented by Arden + White Gallery , Bartelt installed 8 of her understated-yet-colorful paper-and-linen compositions inside the Gores Pavilion , a landmarked home designed by modernist architect — and Philip Johnson collaborator — Landis Gores in 1960. The artworks resonate with both the colors and the geometries found in the home, but they weren’t so much inspired by the architecture as chosen to complement it; if you know Bartelt’s work, you know this has been her visual language for years. As the gallery puts it: “This exhibition is not about illustrating architecture, nor about placing contemporary art within an iconic building. Rather, it reveals a shared architectural sensibility, one rooted in proportion, restraint, and the thoughtful orchestration of material, light, and space.” Walker Street Market Is Turning the Berkshires Into a Contemporary Design Destination At Walker Street Market in Lenox, Mass., the craft-forward fare includes a custom counter by Brian Persico and painting by David Silverstein (top), a side table by Simone Bodmer Turner and lamp by Ashley Joseph Martin (above left), and a teapot by Akira Satake (above right), among many others. For a Summer, the Athens-Based Gallery Antiqua is Trading White Walls for the Deep Blue Sea The Athens-based 20th-century furniture gallery Antiqua is popping up on the Greek island of Antiparos for the summer in a show called “By the Sea.” Photos: Giorgos Sfakianakis One regrettable limitation of having a permanent gallery space is that, regardless of how much exhibition design you can pull off, or how many bizarre interventions ensue, each show still retains the DNA of its enclosure. An Alex Da Corte show at Karma Gallery — even with red carpeting, pink walls, and an upside-down inflatable cat — still feels like a typical Karma Gallery show; heavy curtains or a Do Ho Suh–esque house can’t fool you into thinking you’re not at Jacqueline Sullivan’s. (Perhaps the most successful transformation of a known space I’ve ever seen was Felix Burrichter’s Charlap Hyman & Herrero–designed BLOW-UP exhibition for Friedman Benda , but that’s another story for another day about how 2019 was my favorite year in design.) This is why it’s so exciting when a shop or gallery decides to decamp entirely to a new space, whether for the long haul or even for a few months. There’s a pleasant friction that develops from seeing the same pieces in a new envelope. The Athens-based 20th-century furniture gallery Antiqua is taking full advantage of that friction this summer as they pop up on the island of Antiparos, in a space called Maison Bardot, a cultural center not far from the beach. Maison Bardot’s aesthetic is typically Cycladic — lime and clay surfaces, pigmented terracotta floors, diffused light — so much so that it temporarily scrambled my brain to see pieces like this blue-legged Sottsass bookcase or a laminated wood Mendini chair inside it. But I Could Never Have Anticipated What Would Make It So Great. by Jill Singer If you can believe it, this was my first year attending 3DaysofDesign in Copenhagen, and I went to the fair, now in its 10th year, armed with absurdly high expectations. I knew that just existing in Copenhagen in early June — using Lime bikes to cycle around, drinking natural wine, eating smørrebrød — would set a good baseline for fun. But after my experience at Salone, which I wrote about here , I felt increasingly desperate for Copenhagen to mean something . I told people I was going because, as a chronicler of design fair culture, I felt compelled to see one that had become such a word-of-mouth success. But on a personal level, it’s like I needed Copenhagen to prove to me that design fairs were still worth attending. As hesitant as I am to say this — lest everyone frantically start planning their show next year in Denmark, which is simply not the right move for everyone — Copenhagen actually exceeded my expectations. As I went through the week, seeing the precise things where, to me, Milan fell short — i.e. incredible group shows assembled by designers and brand presentations so intentional they bordered on religious — I began to develop a theory about what made this year in Copenhagen so great. I crystallized it in my group chat. “There was a matriarchal energy to 3Days that stood in stark contrast to Milan,” I wrote. “Women were at the helm of almost every company or exhibition I loved. Not to the exclusion of men at all. But in a way that I have never in my life felt at a design fair.” There were Rhya Johnston-Wallace and Kasia Sznajder, two ex-Frama employees who not only curated their own star exhibitions but also helped organize and promote presentations by a collection of mostly female-led brands or galleries . There were the big Danish brands, from Fredericia to Fritz Hansen, with their new female creative directors. There were exhibitions centered around traditional women’s crafts, like the quilts at Tekla and or the sewing exhibition at Vaerktoj. Photography: © Galerie Patrick Seguin This week Design Miami is taking over Paris’s 7th arrondissement and with it a Jean Prouvé classic. In the garden at Hôtel de Maisons, the hôtel particulier where the fair has based itself since it launched here three years ago, the gallerist Patrick Seguin has installed one of the demountable pavilions Prouvé designed at the end of the Second World War. The 6×6 Demountable House was commissioned by the French government as a temporary, lightweight alternative for postwar homeless communities. And Prouvé, a founding member of the Union of Modern Artists with Le Corbusier , who embraced industrialisation as many designers decried it, was the perfect man to execute it. Here, the installation serves as a reminder that affordable, dignified shelter is never beyond our scope. Photography: © Galerie Patrick Seguin Photography: © Galerie Patrick Seguin 1 of 2 Surrounded by the mansion’s elegant 18th-century limestone walls — onetime home of fashion designer Karl Lagerfeld — Seguin has reinterpreted the structure's interior space. Photography: Marco Galloway When Paul Schärer took over the Swiss manufacturer USM in the 1960s, he commissioned the influential architectect Fritz Haller to design its new headquarters. Haller responded with a flexible, modular chromed framework that could be reconfigured with ball joints to the needs of the office. He then set his mind to furnishing it, and designed a range that could match the new buildings’ sleek and adaptable structure. What he came up with was a system of steel modules that could stack vertically, laterally and elegantly. A design classic with a clean, industrial minimalism and rich powder-coated colour, the USM modular system became a mid-century classic and a staple of functional spaces everywhere. They can recede into the architecture of a space or become luxurious features when displaying collectible objects, flowers, records. But we've never seen it used in this most recent application — as the foundation for this new bar by New York entrepreneur Josh Greenspan. Photography: Marco Galloway 1 of 4 VV's Cocktail Room, named for Greenspan's daughter, Vivienne, was inspired by late nights in New York and omakases in Tokyo . Not so fast, say designers Reports of its death have been greatly exaggerated A London dining room designed by Run For the Hills. Photography: courtesy of Run For the Hills Shifting lifestyle preferences have fuelled popularity for kitchen-diners, breakfast bars and sofa suppers. But does that mean dedicated eating spaces are heading for extinction? While a report by Aviva released last month found that one in five homeowners has repurposed the dining room, it seems not everyone is clamouring to phase them out. A new generation of designers is reimagining the dining room in a convivial, flexible way that’s neither stuffy nor formal — as a place not only for a special occasion but also for a random Tuesday, as a place to quietly gather away from the chaos of the kitchen. ‘If you do a dining room right and make it a space that’s not just for family Christmases, you’ll use it far more than an old-style stuffy space,’ says Anna Burles, cofounder of interiors studio Run For the Hills . ‘Make it cosy, casually glamorous and comfortable enough to feel right for regular, old family dinners — phones and devices left at the door. But also make it the perfect spot for laying out boardgames or a jigsaw or setting up a craft project that’s not in the main kitchen. Gench’s description of the apartment could also be applied to the person who lives there: He’s a reserved and thoughtful man who, in his free time, creates objects with a 3D printer and crafts small lamps and decorative objects out of wood. “He wasn’t looking to create a simply contemporary and functional interior, but instead a space that would truly interest him and reflect his personality,” she says. Artpole gypsum panels add texture to the surfaces, while items from Woon Stores decorate the shelves. Foto: Inna Kablukova The bathroom was expanded, and given the owner’s creative interests, a workspace was a must. Coquery lounge chairs and a Marcel Breuer table. Vitsoe shelves host an Andy Warhol Brillo Box and a Jordan McDonald vase. So me say the world will end in fire/Some say in ice. Those opening lines to Robert Frost’s apocalyptic 1920 poem “Fire and Ice” provided unlikely inspiration for a line of candles created by interior designer Patrick McGrath that will debut this holiday season. items.text: First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos 23 October 2026 • Projects Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, the property will mark the first Hyatt hotel in Turks & Caicos and the first Caribbean island resort for the Andaz brand. The 132-key resort is designed by architecture by RAD Architecture with interiors by Modus Operandi in collaboration with Hyatt. Gently curving with the coastline, the west-facing property will offer a sunset perspective at every touchpoint. Set directly on the white sands of Grace Bay and steps from Bight Reef within Princess Alexandra National Park, Andaz Turks & Caicos will comprise 59 hotel rooms and 73 branded residences, also available for stays, with 10 penthouses featuring their very own rooftop plunge pools. The resort will feature three swimming pools, the 7,000ft 2 Runa Spa & Wellness, four dining concepts, a dedicated Kids Club, tennis and pickleball courts, in addition to ample weddings and event space. The structural narrative of Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay will unfold around an arrival sequence that takes cues from the island’s early history, when visitors arrived exclusively by boat. The entrance will recreate this experience, translating the pier into a long, immersive progression toward Grace Bay. Guests will move along a wood-lined corridor whose framing references the skeleton of an overturned boat. Set 15ft above the sea, the vantage point will immediately give the feeling of floating over the water as panoramic ocean views open up. That connection will continue throughout the interiors, where local stone and rich, natural materials add warmth while shifting hues of blues draw the surrounding waters indoors. The guestrooms’ expansive views and indoor-outdoor living will be balanced by a sense of privacy. Teak and hardwoods, richly textured fabrics and streams of natural light filtering into the bathrooms will create a tactile warmth, while artwork by Caribbean artists and pops of colour will bring the island’s character indoors. A traditional Turks & Caicos dress, distinguished by its colourful stripes representing the individual islands, will serve as a cultural touchpoint for the interiors. The striped pattern is reinterpreted in the wooden headboards, translating a recognisable element of local dress into a subtle design detail. In addition to 59 standard guestrooms, the 73 branded residences include studios as well as one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom layouts, with the largest four-bedroom residences spanning up to 8,336ft 2 of indoor and outdoor space. Each residence will offer a balcony or terrace, indoor-outdoor living spaces and a Bosch-equipped kitchen. items.text: Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma 22 October 2026 • Projects Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary Dolce Vita. Located on the Via Veneto in a building that formerly housed a bank, the hotel features 82 rooms, a rooftop, a suspended swimming pool, and an interior scheme by Rodolphe Parente. “For Experimental Roma, I did not want to recreate or imitate a nostalgic vision of Rome,” says Parente. “Instead, I wanted to create a living tribute, a free interpretation expressed through materials and space. A place charged with the same tensions that define Rome itself: sacred and profane, splendour and decadence.” In the lobby, the designer has curated an intimate interior that blends heritage and reinvention. Italian opulence is revisited through a French lens and the legacies of great Italian masters – such as Gio Ponti, Carlo Scarpa and Luigi Caccia Dominioni – are referenced through subtle nods to the 1970s: chrome tubing, disco-inspired accents, lurex carpets, a sculptural staircase and rich and textured materials. Throughout the restaurant and public spaces, enveloping banquettes, quilted drapery and exposed beams pay homage to Italian cinema, while the rooftop features an expansive bar overlooking the Eternal City, a swimming pool and a terrace. The hotel’s 82 rooms are divided into two principal categories. The first evokes the theatrical Roman bedroom, bathed in light filtered through interior shutters. Large blocks of colour, dramatic headboards inspired by antique drapery and a sense of romantic intimacy reminiscent of Villa Medici define these spaces. Colourful basins, vibrant details and a richer, more expressive design language create a dialogue between ancient Roman baroque influences and the hedonism of the 1970s. The second category embraces a more refined, almost futuristic aesthetic. Mineral patinas, two-tone lacquered ceilings and ribbed stainless-steel headboards resembling contemporary sculptures create a contemplative atmosphere. Artworks throughout the rooms evoke the worlds of Cy Twombly, Christo, Ugo Ferranti and the Yvon Lambert Gallery. The bathrooms are conceived as contrasting boxes, balancing warm wood with cool stone, raw materials with bespoke graphic details. “Experimental Roma is a hotel of inverted perspectives,” Parente concludes. “A French interpretation of Italy; an Italy reinvented through materials, textures and light. Noble materials interact with reimagined industrial elements. Marble converses with folded stainless steel, while terracotta tones vibrate against polished metal surfaces. items.text: The Romeo Collection announces expansion to Massa Lubrense - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search The Romeo Collection announces expansion to Massa Lubrense 21 October 2026 • Projects The Romeo Collection has announced its third hotel, Romeo Massa Lubrense, which is set to debut in May 2027. The new destination emerges as an exclusive retreat suspended between architecture and nature. Designed by architect Kengo Kuma, Romeo Massa Lubrense establishes an escape centred around reclaimed time, privacy and deep connection to place. Tucked away in a secluded natural reserve in Punta San Lorenzo, the closest point of the coastline to Capri, Romeo Massa Lubrense is built directly onto a private natural fjord. Reimagined from the historic 1963 Hotel Delfino with a rigorous commitment to environmental restoration, Kuma maximises the property’s connection to its surroundings, creating a contemporary sanctuary that blends architecture and nature. The design is rooted in Kuma’s philosophy of dissolving architecture into the landscape and the Japanese concept of Ma (間), that emptiness is not absence but a silent presence. The design palette relies on warm, organic tones and natural Mediterranean materials, including local tuff, travertine, American walnut and matte ceramics. These materials, paired with transparency and the soft curves Kuma is known for, ensure the architecture achieves a sense of ‘visual subtraction’, relieved of clutter. The boundaries of the 63 rooms and suites dissolve entirely with true indoor-outdoor living, with the view over the Gulf blurring the separation between infinity pool and sea, and a minimalistic design bound by the natural surroundings that ensures the property becomes one with the sea, light, and nature that define the cliffside. “Our vision for The Romeo Collection has always been to create experiences driven by their destinations, and Massa Lubrense captures the authentic, slow-living spirit of the Italian coast like nowhere else,” says Alfredo Romeo, founder of The Romeo Collection. “I am thrilled to soon share this project, which will marry a rare, dramatic natural landscape with unparalleled design and hospitality. We are creating an ultra-exclusive retreat that I believe will truly redefine the luxury resort experience in Italy.” italy Kengo Kuma new hotel Romeo Collection The Romeo Collection Related Posts 22 August 2025 Radisson Collection debuts in Hungary 24 April 2023 The Romeo Collection expanding Italian portfolio 3 March 2014 Starwood announces five new projects in China Sign up for Sleeper's free email alerts Home About Media Pack AHEAD Subscribe Contact Cookie Policy © 2026 Sleeper Media Ltd. items.summary:
Paragon Studio is taking hotel fitness out of the basement with In-Suite, a range of fitness equipment designed for guestroom-based […] 
 The post  Paragon Studio to debut In-Suite collection at HIX Europe 2026  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Paragon Studio to debut In-Suite collection at HIX Europe 2026 - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Paragon Studio to debut In-Suite collection at HIX Europe 2026 20 October 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Paragon Studio is taking hotel fitness out of the basement with In-Suite, a range of fitness equipment designed for guestroom-based workouts. Making its debut at HIX Europe 2026 at Stand C30, In-Suite will officially launch as the global wellness economy reaches a record $6.8 trillion, with wellness tourism alone valued at $894 billion, according to the Global Wellness Institute. The range, targeting luxury hotels who invest consciously in wellness, combines three elements: the kit, the content and the service. Each is designed to work with the others, so the room adapts to the guest’s habits and not the other way round. For hotels, it offers a wellness proposition that sits inside the suite itself, without the need for additional square footage elsewhere on the property. Research for In-Suite has been developed with the modern traveller in mind, someone who doesn’t want to use the gym but still values exercise, movement and routine. This guest profile is more likely to enjoy practicing mindful movement, such as yoga, Pilates and light mobility. The collection comprises movement, recovery and strength kits, housed in a foam insert cut to fit the room’s existing drawers, in a wooden tray, or delivered to order. Each kit carries a laser-etched QR plaque linking guests to a video library of strength, Pilates and recovery sessions, which can be branded, subtitled and filmed on site in the hotel’s own rooms. Because the inserts use joinery already in place, they can be retrofitted into rooms that are open and trading. What’s more, every piece has its own cut-out, so housekeeping can see if anything is missing. Paragon Studio will launch with three core options: the Movement Kit, the Recovery Kit and the Lite Kit. The Movement Kit includes hand-weights, a kettlebell, resistance bands and a cork yoga mat and block, all housed within a bespoke insert, while the Recovery Kit includes a massage gun, massage ball, red LED light therapy panel and a roller. Additionally, a Lite Kit, featuring a pared-back selection of equipment and select content library, is available to hotel operators seeking a comprehensive wellness offering across all room categories. At HIX Europe, the collection will be shown as a separate tray and in a bed created in partnership with Naturalmat, its drawer built into the base. The pieces will demonstrate how far In-Suite can be tailored: inserts can be cut to fit furniture already in the room, or designed into new pieces from the outset to any specification a project calls for. Throughout the two-day show, Paragon Studio’s stand will double as a recording studio, with industry podcasts recorded live in conversation with designers, operators and developers on how wellness works

items.title: Astro Lighting presents Coastal collection
items.summary:
Astro Lighting presents the Coastal collection, a lighting range developed with coastal hospitality in mind. In such properties, lighting plays […] 
 The post  Astro Lighting presents Coastal collection  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Astro Lighting presents Coastal collection - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Astro Lighting presents Coastal collection 19 October 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Astro Lighting presents the Coastal collection, a lighting range developed with coastal hospitality in mind. In such properties, lighting plays a vital role in how a place is experienced after dark. It guides arrival, supports movement, defines outdoor areas and helps create the atmosphere guests associate with a memorable stay. From hotel entrances and terraces to pathways, balconies and restaurants by the water, the right light can bring clarity and warmth to spaces that are designed to feel open, relaxed and connected to their surroundings. Yet the lighting brand highlights how the environments that make these settings so compelling are often the same ones that make them difficult to design for. Salt-laden air, moisture, heat, wind and UV exposure can all place pressure on exterior materials and finishes. The challenge is not limited to the coast. Hotels, resorts and hospitality venues in other demanding settings, such as humid spa environments, exposed terraces and outdoor dining areas, also require lighting that can perform reliably while maintaining the quality of the design. According to Astro, this is where performance and atmosphere need to work together. In hospitality, exterior lighting is rarely specified for function alone. It has to support the architecture, contribute to the guest journey and sit comfortably within the wider material palette. At the same time, it must be able to withstand the conditions of its location. When these requirements are considered from the outset, durability becomes part of the design rather than a technical compromise. Astro’s Coastal collection has been developed with this balance in mind. Designed for coastal and other challenging exterior environments, the range brings together refined architectural forms with materials selected for long-term resilience. Across the collection, concrete, ceramic, PVD finishes and marine-grade stainless steel each offer a different response to exposure, helping designers specify lighting that feels appropriate to the setting while giving operators confidence in its performance. Material choice is especially important in hospitality, where every visible detail contributes to the overall character of the scheme. Concrete brings texture, solidity and a natural connection to architecture, particularly in spaces shaped by plaster, stone, timber and pale exterior surfaces. Ceramic offers a clean and enduring quality, while PVD finishes and stainless-steel support resistance to corrosion, wear and discolouration in more exposed locations. These details are not intended to dominate the design, their value lies in how quietly they support it. For Astro, this relationship between appearance and endurance is fundamental. items.text: andBeyond Xaranna Okavango Delta Lodge to undergo renovation - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search andBeyond Xaranna Okavango Delta Lodge to undergo renovation 19 October 2026 • Projects andBeyond is set to reopen one of its Botswana properties as andBeyond Xaranna Okavango Delta Lodge in August 2027 following an extensive rebuild. Set within an exclusive 90,500 hectare concession in the Okavango Delta, Xaranna’s interiors, envisioned by multidisciplinary design practice LIFE Interiors Architecture Strategic Design, will bring the landscape into every aspect of the guest experience. The redesigned lodge will reflect the unhurried qualities of the Okavango and the ever-changing relationship between land and water. Creative inspirations such as the gentle movement of the floodplains, the linearity of reeds and Botswana’s rich weaving traditions will be translated through the intentional layering of natural materials and tactile finishes such as subtle rope detailing throughout the lodge. A softened palette of sage and forest green will accentuate the blonde linen and textured weaves, while timber and beaten brass bring warmth and depth. With carefully considered connections to the landscape, these raw and refined elements will allow the Delta’s changing character to remain present throughout the lodge; effortlessly complementing one another. Reimagined guest areas have been conceived to encourage a natural flow between the interiors and the landscape beyond. Arriving by boat or vehicle, guests will be welcomed into the lodge’s arrival experience before moving through a series of open, light-filled interiors that gradually reveal the Delta, culminating in generous lounge and living areas framed by uninterrupted views. At the heart of the lodge, the main guest area will serve as Xaranna’s social heartbeat, bringing together lounge, dining and creative spaces in a setting inspired by the Setswana tradition of gathering. Guests can spend evenings beneath the stars in the traditional boma, settle into the library, or enjoy carefully selected wines in the sculptural wine bodega before ascending to the stargazing nest for panoramic views across the floodplains and night sky. The lodge has been reimagined to offer an even greater sense of space and privacy, featuring nine expansive Suites, each measuring 160m² and offering elevated comfort through thoughtfully designed living areas, personal bar and two-way fireplace. Each air-conditioned Suite will extend effortlessly outdoors to include spacious seating areas, a private pool and shaded sala. A new two-bedroom Family Suite of 404 m² will further enhance the lodge’s offering for families and small groups seeking exclusive accommodation. items.text: MGallery expands in China with Financial City Chengdu opening - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search MGallery expands in China with Financial City Chengdu opening 15 October 2026 • Projects MGallery Collection , Accor’s portfolio of storied boutique hotels, has announced the official opening of Financial City Chengdu – MGallery Collection, the newest address in Greater China. Nestled in the heart of Chengdu Financial City, the hotel becomes the third MGallery property in Chengdu, enjoying a prime urban location at the crossroads of the city’s economic and urban energy. Reflecting MGallery Collection’s philosophy, where every hotel is rooted in a meaningful story, destination and spirit, Financial City Chengdu – MGallery Collection brings the cultural character of Chengdu into a contemporary urban setting. Designed by Australian design firm Stack Studio, the hotel’s aesthetic is inspired by the poetic imagery of Tang Dynasty poet Zhang Ji’s famous Song of Chengdu, evoking the whimsical beauty of ‘wandering into a hidden lychee grove’. The design narrative begins on arrival, beneath the branches of a century-old local lychee tree rooted in the ground floor. Seven floors above, Sky Garden continues this journey upwards, unfolding as a lush rooftop garden where greenery, open air and the changing light of Chengdu create a quiet pause above the city. The hotel offers 155 guestrooms and suites, intentionally designed to reflect the character of the city. Continuing the overall design narrative, the guestrooms translate the beauty of river mists, mountain fogs and crimson sunsets into contemporary living spaces. For meetings and social events, the hotel features a multi-functional event space totalling approximately 480m 2 , highly adaptable for corporate gatherings, refined banquets and intimate private celebrations. The hotel’s Fitness Centre features floor-to-ceiling panoramic windows opening onto an outdoor terrace, creating a bright and restorative space for guests to stay active and recharge. In line with Accor’s global sustainability commitments, Financial City Chengdu – MGallery Collection integrates eco-conscious practices throughout its daily operations. Key initiatives include a comprehensive plastic-reduction program, smart in-room energy management and an energy-efficient building envelope featuring insulated Low-E glass curtain walls. items.text: Ora Hospitality to debut new ultra-luxury brand on Mykonos - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search Ora Hospitality to debut new ultra-luxury brand on Mykonos 14 October 2026 • Projects Ora Hospitality – the design-driven hospitality arm of global real estate leader Ora Developers – has announced the launch of a new ultra-luxury hospitality and lifestyle brand, with a flagship property scheduled to open on Mykonos in May 2027. The yet-to-be-named brand aims to bring a fresh approach to ultra-luxury hospitality, balancing exploration and discovery with moments of tranquillity, escape and renewal. Across its future portfolio, each property will weave art, architecture, music, wellness and local gastronomy into a distinctive guest experience, defined by intuitive, personal service. With an experience-led approach, the brand will also partner with leading global names across wellness, F&B and lifestyle to create elevated experiences that feel connected to each destination. Set on an elevated hillside rising above Kalo Livadi Bay, the brand’s debut €100 million resort on Mykonos will occupy a largely undeveloped stretch of prime coastline, offering uninterrupted views across the Aegean Sea. The property will feature 93 keys, comprising 60 rooms, 28 suites and five exclusive villas, arranged village-style with sea views and private outdoor spaces. Founder Naguib Sawiris is personally guiding every aspect of the project’s design and concept. His connection to Mykonos is deeply personal, shaped by decades of memories on the island and by returning year after year with his family. items.text: HBA transforms Taichung department store into Art Deco escape - Sleeper Home Stories About Issue Library Events Diary AHEAD Subscribe Contact Search HBA transforms Taichung department store into Art Deco escape 13 October 2026 • Projects Designed by Studio HBA Singapore, Oku Hotel Taichung transforms the former Sakurada Department Store – a landmark in Taichung’s historic Central District – into a richly layered boutique hospitality destination. Guided by the concept of ‘The Department of Travellers’ Tales’, the design imagines the hotel as the collection of a fictional traveller, where memories, discoveries and treasured objects gathered from around the world are woven into the guest experience. Through a sophisticated blend of Art Deco influences, European vintage glamour and contemporary luxury, the 80-key hotel bridges past and present while celebrating the ongoing revitalisation of Taichung’s historic urban core. Rather than erasing its history, Studio HBA Singapore embraced the former department store’s legacy and reinterpreted it as a contemporary destination for exploration and discovery. The result is a hospitality experience that retains the spirit of the original building while introducing a renewed sense of purpose within the city’s evolving cultural landscape. Guests arrive at a triple-height lobby anchored by soaring arches, lustrous metallic finishes and custom-crafted details. The space unfolds around Ailìse Bar’s dramatic multi-storey liquor tower, which rises through the centre of the atrium, while elegant galleries and mezzanine walkways overlook the lobby below. Framed by elegant metalwork, mirrored surfaces and sculptural lighting, the bar is anchored by a vibrant emerald-green fluted counter topped with pristine white stone and complemented by plush velvet stools, evoking the glamour and sophistication of the Art Deco era. Throughout the hotel, Studio HBA Singapore reinterprets French Art Deco through a contemporary lens. Symmetrical geometric patterns, fluted metallic details, bronze accents and decorative screening establish a strong architectural language, while a rich palette of deep navy blue, peacock green, warm gold and polished stone brings depth and character to every space. Herringbone timber flooring, luxurious velvet textiles and layered lighting further enhance the feeling of timeless sophistication, evoking the glamour and romance of the golden age of travel. The guestrooms continue the narrative of discovery and collection, offering a residential retreat that balances heritage-inspired detailing with contemporary comfort. Floor-to-ceiling windows framed by dramatic velvet drapery create a sense of quiet grandeur, while bespoke furnishings, intricate geometric wall features and refined gold accents reinforce the hotel’s Art Deco identity. The studio established take-back agreements with nine manufacturers: Pfleiderer, Granorte, Shards, Søuld, ClayTec, STRAMEN.TEC, Tarkett, Bosch, and Vitra, ensuring that interior building products can be reclaimed and reprocessed into new materials at the end of their lifecycle. items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Experimental Roma  – a French interpretation of Italy  
  Experimental Roma  – a French interpretation of Italy  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Experimental Roma – a French interpretation of Italy • Hotel Designs Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Experimental Roma – a French interpretation of Italy WORDS BY Pauline Brettell October 23, 2026 Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Atkinson Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Experimental Roma – a French interpretation of Italy Experimental’s new Roman address on the legendary Via Veneto is open – a vibrant, sensual and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary Dolce Vita. Rodolphe Parente, Interior Architect of Experimental Roma, shares his design vision… Rome is a city I dreamed about for a long time before I had the opportunity to work there. It is extravagant, spectacular and paradoxical. A concentration of beauty and ruins. A living museum, yet also a vibrant, pulsating city carrying the legacy of multiple civilizations: a layered composition of eras, styles and desires. Rodolphe Parente | Image credit: Experimental Roma Image credit: Experimental Roma Via Veneto is where this project was born . The legendary street of La Dolce Vita, synonymous with the glamour of 1950s and 1960s Italy, where paparazzi chased movie stars emerging from grand hotels and actresses in extraordinary gowns stepped out of Alfa Romeo taxis. A street of fantasy, still permeated by the aura of Italian cinema. A place where sensuality, elegance and spirituality coexist. Rome is not a postcard. It is an inner labyrinth. Once you begin to truly look at it, you see all human societies speaking to one another across time. There is La Grande Bellezza, of course – the celebration, the aesthetics, the solitude, the memory. But there is also Pasolini, with his raw perspective on social tensions and spirituality. For Experimental Roma, I did not want to recreate or imitate a nostalgic vision of Rome . Instead, I wanted to create a living tribute, a free interpretation expressed through materials and space. A place charged with the same tensions that define Rome itself: sacred and profane, splendour and decadence. Image credit: Experimental Roma An atmosphere of light and shadow Upon entering the lobby, the bustling city outside gives way to an intimate interior where heritage and reinvention blend. Italian opulence is revisited through a distinctly French lens and the legacies of great Italian masters – such as Gio Ponti, Carlo Scarpa and Luigi Caccia

items.text: Inside the ceramic craft behind the Japanese WASHLET by TOTO Subscribe News Resource Hub Hotel Suppliers Hotel Industry Network Supplier News On The Boards Hotel Reviews Spotlight On In Conversation Hotel Designs LABS SPACE Magazine DESIGN POD Guide To Hotel Design Editor’s Picks Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Newsletter Contact Us SUBSCRIBE Hotel Designs Hotel Designs News Hotel Suppliers On The Boards SPACE Magazine Events Industry Events MEET UP London MEET UP North The Brit List Awards Accessible Design Talks Hotel Summit Interior Design & Architecture Summit Product watch: inside the ceramic craft behind the Japanese WASHLET from TOTO WORDS BY Sienna Shipton October 23, 2026 Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Atkinson Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Product watch: inside the ceramic craft behind the Japanese WASHLET from TOTO Behind TOTO’s WASHLET lies a lesser-known story of ceramic, from the materials and craftsmanship to the precision that shapes its distinctive white form… Best known for bringing advanced Japanese shower toilet technology into the bathroom, TOTO has established itself as a leading manufacturer in the category. Yet, behind its signature WASHLET lies something altogether more fundamental: ceramic. Hotel Designs takes a closer look at the material, craftsmanship and precision behind its distinctive white form. For all its associations with advanced bathroom technology, the WASHLET begins with clay – a simple, natural material shaped, refined and transformed by fire into something enduring. The ceramic bowl beneath is made from the same family of materials as everyday tableware, but engineered for a very different purpose. Through precision moulding, the organic, pebble-like silhouette takes shape, creating the distinctive white form beneath the WASHLET. Image credit: TOTO Achieving that consistent finish begins with the raw materials themselves. TOTO sources locally wherever possible, while also procuring specific materials internationally when required to meet its standards. The same level of care extends to transport: materials are typically shipped in food-grade containers to prevent contamination. During the container shortages that followed the Covid-19 pandemic, these food-grade containers were not always available. In those cases, TOTO used standard containers lined with protective sheeting to create a clean internal environment and prevent impurities from coming into contact with the materials. This attention to detail helps safeguard the quality at every stage. The production process begins with more than 20 natural raw materials, including clay, feldspar and pottery stone. Custom-designed furniture echoes the location’s architectural richness, whilst the SpaceInvader team worked closely with art consultants Studio Graphite to create a gallery approach to the new art in the rooms, paying homage both to near neighbour Tate Modern and the area’s predominant graffiti and wall-art. “Our approach to the Hilton London Bankside expansion was rooted in storytelling”, John Williams, SpaceInvader Founder/Director commented. “As well as research into local history, we walked endlessly round the area to absorb its heritage and character in order to infuse every aspect of the design – from colour, textures and materials right down to the shape of bespoke furniture and fringing and piping details – with a sense of place, referencing the Thames and Tate Modern as well as Shakespeare’s Globe and the area’s theatrical heritage.” Image credit: Ben Sage / Hilton Bankside The new extension – by architects Studio Moren – sees the highly-popular hotel adding a new ninth floor with sweeping views across Bankside and the surrounding London skyline, as well as new rooms and corridors to floors four, five and six, bringing the hotel’s total offer to 368 rooms. Building a hotel into a working farm with a 500-year history, Creative Director Paul Eldwin Glade has allowed the landscape, local materials and the people who know it best to shape the experience – from estate-sourced stone and farm-grown wool to a regenerative approach that connects hospitality with agriculture. Image credit: Jon Tonks Hotel Designs: Fowlescombe Farm feels less like a hotel placed on a farm and more like a farm that has evolved into a hotel. What was the starting point for the design, and how important was it to allow the land to lead the creative process? Paul Eldwin Glade: The starting point was absolutely the farm, and how it already worked. Fowlescombe has been farmed for around 500 years, so the idea wasn’t to impose a hotel onto it, but to understand what was already here and work out what we could preserve, bring forward or carefully add. I think you have to look at a place properly before you decide what it should become. I spent a lot of time simply getting to know Fowlescombe, the buildings, landscape, light, weather, materials, people and the way the farm actually works. If the farm is working regeneratively, the hotel should follow the same principle. Anything we add should strengthen rather than draw down from what is already here. The farm gives the hotel its purpose, and the hotel supports the farm in return. I wanted the design to make Fowlescombe more fully itself rather than turn it into something else. The newly designed Garden Room has been conceived as an immersive cigar and whisky lounge – a richly layered, dark and atmospheric destination designed to elevate the guest experience. Intimate yet welcoming, the space offers hotel guests and visitors a sophisticated retreat that remains connected to its verdant setting and immediate proximity to Hyde Park. Craftsmanship: A focus on integrity of material application and pride in execution, delivering a level of quality befitting a leading British institution. Timeless: Drawing on The Lanesborough’s heritage to create a design that feels enduring rather than trend-led. The experience begins at the threshold. Guests are welcomed through a bespoke timber and brushed brass portal, where carefully crafted joinery frames a curated display of the world’s finest cigars and rare whiskies. A Pierre Frey inset carpet defines the entrance, while Portland Limestone, Verde Antique and Nero Marquina stone flooring establishes an immediate sense of gravitas and permanence. Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo Tilman Fertitta’s Latest Buy Is a Lucrative Italian Legend Across From Lincoln Center NYC Restaurant News Tilman Fertitta’s Latest Buy Is a Lucrative Italian Legend Across From Lincoln Center The billionaire restaurateur takes over the bankrupt hospitality company, but some locations aren’t along for the ride by Tierney Plumb Oct 22, 2026, 3:42 PM UTC Facebook Link Cafe Fiorello Tierney Plumb is an editor of Eater’s Northeast region, covering D.C., Boston, Philly, and New York. Cafe Fiorello , NYC’s iconic Italian chophouse across from the Lincoln Center since 1974 on the Upper West Side, has a new owner. Texas mega-billionaire restaurateur (and NBA Houston Rockets owner) Tilman Fertitta, is taking over bankrupt Fireman Hospitality Group ’s three Manhattan mainstays — Trattoria dell’ Arte, Fiorello’s, and Bond 45 — as part of a newly announced $22 million purchase in conjunction with Ciao Hospitality Group, which will act as the new operator, per the New York Post , who reports it as a Landry’s acquisition. Some of the restaurants in the Fireman portfolio aren’t joining the new family, including D.C.’s recently opened Cafe Fiorello and Fiorella Italian Kitchen & Pizzeria — both closing this October as part of the deal, as Eater DC first reported. Fertitta (and his company) scooping up legacy restaurants has been a trend, with his purchase of Keens steakhouse in New York and Union Oyster House in Boston, both of which were founded in the 1800s. Fertitta’s Titanic-sized restaurant portfolio includes steakhouse chains under the Landry’s umbrella, which include Morton’s, Mastro’s, Del Frisco’s, Strip House; Mexican cafe chain Dos Caminos; and sushi bar Blue Fin. He’s also a part owner of New York’s Catch Group, which includes scene-y spots like Corner Store , the Eighty Six , Or’esh , and Cafe Charmant. The sceney impresarios behind Los Angeles company the H.Wood Group are making their first mark on New York City this fall. They’re opening a spinoff of their modern supper club restaurant, Delilah , with Lady Delilah in Chelsea at 353 W. 14th Street, near Ninth Avenue on Tuesday, November 3. Out in Los Angeles, the H.Wood Group runs flashy spots known for its no-photos policy and attracting celebrities such as Beyoncé, Jay-Z, Kylie and Kendall Jenner, and Drake. Co-founders John Terzian and Brian Toll opened Delilah in 2016, followed by locations in Las Vegas, Miami, and Dallas. They also ran Delilah as a summer residency out on Montauk. Back in New York, Lady Delilah’s 10,000-square-foot subterranean space takes on an Art Deco feel, with an archway entrance with white tiles mimicking New York City subways, along with vintage oak details, plush seating, chandeliers, and tiled vaulted ceilings. There’s the main dining room with space for live music and performances, along with two private dining rooms. And, yes, it’ll uphold that policy of not letting people take photos. Lady Delilah’s bar. Michael Clifford for the H.Wood Group “Our vision was to design a space that celebrates the theatrical romance of the past, where eating, drinking and dancing come together effortlessly,” Terzian and Toll write in the press release. H.Wood’s culinary director, chef Michael Teich, is overseeing the menu, which will lean modern American bistro. The bar will serve cocktails, spirits, and fancy bottle service. Facebook Link A piece of sushi from Mitani. | Daniel Kruglikov Facebook Link Currently, there’s a four-year waitlist to score one of the six seats at chef Yasuhiko Mitani’s Yotsuya sushi counter , the famously inaccessible, introduction-only restaurant he opened in Tokyo 20 years ago. In New York, it’s considerably easier to eat Mitani’s sushi. All you need to do is hop on Tock and book seats for his newest Midtown restaurant — for a price. In May, the chef quietly opened Mitani New York , his first U.S. restaurant, inside Midtown’s Lotte New York Palace hotel (455 Madison Avenue, at 50th Street). The seasonal dinner tasting menu costs $700, including tip, for roughly six appetizers and 10 to 12 pieces of sushi. The meal is built entirely around Japanese seafood sourced at fish-market auctions. At its core is what he calls “Mariage,” Mitani’s approach to pairing courses with wines, sake, and tea. Serving wine with sushi is hardly new: High-end counters including the Upper East Side’s Sushi Noz and Midtown’s Jōji have incorporated serious French wines into their omakases for years. What distinguishes Mitani is the caliber of what’s poured by the glass — and how those drinks transform each course. At Mitani, the pairings include aged Champagne, Burgundy, and Sauternes, with bottles such as 2002 Cristal and 1981 Château d’Yquem opened for individual pours. Mitani’s original restaurant in Japan holds a Tabelog Gold award . He opened it in 2006, followed by Kioicho Mitani Honten in 2016 and Kioicho Mitani Bettei in 2021. Regulars book Honten about a year ahead and Bettei about 10 months out. Daniel Kruglikov Why diners can get a Mitani reservation in Manhattan Mitani New York has two private dining rooms, each with a six-seat, L-shaped hinoki counter. Executive chef Kazuya Tsurta leads the cream-colored Oh Room. He spent five years at Kioicho Mitani and works alongside another Mitani alum, Daichi Shimamiya.

AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. The iconic Original Pantry Cafe will reopen on November 19, and the timing couldn’t be better for Los Angeles. After the century-old diner closed in March 2025, the owners announced that the Downtown restaurant would reopen, but no one knew when. With restaurant closures continuing at a constant pace in 2026, the return of one of Southern California’s oldest restaurants comes as welcome news, first reported by SF Gate . The Original Pantry Cafe will collaborate with the nonprofit Hope the Mission , a prominent service provider for the unhoused in Greater Los Angeles. Real estate entrepreneur Leo Pustilnikov became the new owner in September 2025. SF Gate’s report also states every meal will help fund the nonprofit while providing job training and support to those caught up in the cycle of home insecurity. Some former Original Pantry employees, many of whom worked at the restaurant for decades, will also return to work, as Pustilnikov has struck a deal with the hospitality workers union, Unite Here Local 11. The Original Pantry debuted in 1924 on the corner of Figueroa and Ninth Streets. Former LA mayor Richard Riordan purchased the restaurant in 1981; when it closed its doors on March 2, 2025, two years after Riordan’s death, a conflict between then-owners the Richard J. Riordan family trust and Unite Here Local 11 over allegations that the closure would violate federal labor law remained. The trust alleged at the time that the primary reason for the closure was to “maximize the value of the real estate.” Longtime fans waited in line for hours over the final weekend for a last taste of the homey diner’s ham steak and eggs, steak, pancakes, fried potatoes, and crunchy coleslaw. Previously, he was the lead editor of Eater’s Southern California/Southwest region. He has covered dining, restaurants, food culture, and nightlife in Los Angeles since 2008. Sign up for his weekly newsletter, Kangtown . I like to think of the restaurant world like sports: there are heroes and villains, legends and heels. And then there are the GOATs. I love thinking about the Greatest of All Time in particular because they help define what it means to be fed and to find community. To me, the greatest restaurants have staying power, influence, quality, and relevance, year in and year out. With almost two decades of exploring this city’s restaurants, I feel it’s time to start naming some of the GOATs of Los Angeles, places that only exist here and create a distinct cultural significance. Sign up for the Kang Town newsletter This post originally appeared in my Kang Town newsletter, where I cover all things dining in the West. Sign up here to get my latest stories. I’m calling this my Pantheon of LA Restaurants (not to be confused with my Pantheon of Animals , a deep cut ). My first inductee: the stately and timeless Jar in Beverly Grove. Founded by chef Suzanne Tracht, Jar celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, and it’s hard to think of a restaurant that has navigated so much while keeping so closely to its original course. Chef and owner Brian Bornemann’s charming, almost 40-seat restaurant is barely a three-minute walk from his noted seafood restaurant, Crudo e Nudo . Here, Bornemann draws on his personal connections with vendors to keep prices as low as possible for diners while maintaining high quality. The result is a compelling eight pastas prepared on site; an enjoyable selection of starters (many sourced from the Santa Monica Farmers Market); good-to-share main dishes; French, Italian, and California wines; and a cocktail menu that rivals any other in the Southland. Bornemann grew up on Ocean Park in Santa Monica; he created Bar Fortuna to make dining out in his neighborhood affordable and accessible. “There’s some good pasta options in town, but they’re either wildly expensive or dinner time only,” says Bornemann. “I don’t want to replicate a Roman street food dish and charge $34 for it. We also chose a smaller space to keep our team focused on quality. Facebook Link Little Luck , the newest restaurant by the Hwood Group, opened on Monday, October 19, in West Hollywood. It’s a compelling flip of the former Bootsy Bellows nightclub, now a modern izakaya by chef Erik Idos (Jean-Georges, Nobu), who recently moved back to his native Los Angeles. Little Luck represents a return for the entire team, in fact. Even the concept looks back to a former era in Los Angeles: the early 2000s, when vibey Asian restaurants were the most innovative in the city. Back then, spots like Koi , Katana , and the influential, now-shuttered Geisha House demonstrated that Asian food could venture beyond basic sushi rolls and casual fusion fare into specialty rolls, elevated pan-Asian dishes, and inventive drinks. These restaurants leaned into moody lighting, sexy design, and ample music programming. Little Luck will take a more contemporary approach, according to Hwood Group co-founder John Terzian. “A big thing for us is to develop concepts inspired by things we love and fill a void,” says Terzian. “We live and breathe West Hollywood, have been in that space for 13 years, plus clubs and lounges on Sunset and in surrounding areas. Coming up as promoters 30 years ago, the best food was Asian cuisine. It’s the right time to do a new version and homage to what it was back then.” Terzian and fellow founder Brian Toll recruited Idos, whose menu starts with snacks like egg salad on milk bread, to which caviar can be added upon request. Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Dining Reports Henrietta Is a Casually Excellent Neighborhood Restaurant The restaurant and market has a winning formula for the south Echo Park strip by Rebecca Roland and Ben Mesirow Updated Oct 20, 2026, 7:07 PM UTC Facebook Link Half chicken. Danielle Adams In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Henrietta , a charming all-day deli, market, and restaurant, lives on the edge of Echo Park and Westlake in the same complex as Clark Street Bakery and a Good Used Book. Owner Max Lesser is a veteran of Chicago’s the Publican and Chi Spacca here in Los Angeles; chef Alexis Brown previously worked at the now-closed Italian institution Alimento. During the day, the restaurant serves sandwiches on bread from neighboring Clark Street Bakery, along with drip coffee, hibiscus lemonade, and wine. After dark, Henrietta becomes a cozy, candlelit bistro, serving some of Los Angeles’s best roast chickens as part of a menu that reflects the bounty of California cooking and produce. With a laid-back, light-filled dining room and a dish lineup that works for a quick lunch or languid dinner, Henrietta has quickly established itself as a place where it’s easy to become a regular. What to order During the day, find sandwiches on Clark Street bread, like the chicken Milanese, which tucks a slice of crispy, breaded chicken between radicchio blanketed in Caesar aioli, and the Shredder, stacked with spicy capicola, Comté, and dill pickles. Everyone, their mother, and their mother’s restaurant seem to be serving crudo in Los Angeles — the dish’s ubiquity makes it easy to dismiss on menus as just another sliced-fish situation. Luckily, that’s not the case at Henrietta, which cranks up the acidity and heat; ruby-red pieces of tuna bathe in Fresno chile and citrus for a punchy bite that lingers once the plate is clean. Beef tartare toast will appeal to both seasoned raw-beef fans and those who are just tartare-curious, with smoky romesco slathered on a toasted slice of sourdough and dollops of crema. Distinctly unphotogenic ricotta dumplings, oblong beige lumps in a brownish broth, make up for their homeliness with comforting depth.

Eater.com Subscribe to Kangtown Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube RSS Eater Eater logo Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin Pop-Ups Eater Bang Bang Is Headed to Austin For one night only, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar are joining forces for a two-dinner-one-night feast by Eater Staff Aug 13, 2026, 10:55 PM UTC Facebook Link Eater’s Bang Bang dinner series is heading to Austin, bringing together two of the city’s most exciting restaurants under one roof for one night only. On August 19, Nixta Taqueria and Lao’d Bar will collaborate on a two-part, six-course dinner that gives diners a chance to explore Mexican and Laotian cooking back-to-back, through bold flavors, shared traditions, and personal storytelling. The evening will open with Chef Edgar Rico’s signature masa-driven cooking, including duck carnitas tacos and Denver steak aguachile. Chef Bob Somsith will follow with dishes inspired by the flavors of Laos, from shrimp ceviche with fried stuffed shrimp head to a fish laab tostada. And expect a delightful collaborative dessert showcasing the best of both restaurants. “I’ve always believed food is one of the best ways to tell your story,” says Bob Somsith at Lao’d Bar. “I’m excited to share the kitchen with Edgar and explore the common threads between Lao and Mexican cuisine. Different histories, different flavors, but the same belief that food has the power to bring people together.” Chef Rico from Nixta agrees. “Even though our cultures are oceans apart, they share so many of the same values: hospitality, honoring those who came before us, and creating flavor bombs that stop you in your tracks.” Tickets are selling out fast, so if you’re in Austin on August 19, get yours today . And download the Eater app to hear about more great events like this. See you at the Bang Bang. items.title: Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park
items.summary: The best hotels, lodges, and cabins for a trip to the Last Frontier.
items.text: Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park | Condé Nast Traveler Skip to main content Condé Nast Traveler Condé Nast Traveler Inspiration Destinations Places to Stay News & Advice Shopping RCA 2026 Plan Your Trip Search Newsletters Account Menu Menu Condé Nast Traveler Account Search Menu Menu Plan Your Trip Inspiration Chevron Destinations Chevron Places to Stay News & Advice Chevron Curated Escapes Shopping Chevron RCA 2026 MORE Cruise Video Women Who Travel Search Search Newsletters Menu Search Close North America Chevron United States Chevron Alaska Chevron Denali Places to Stay Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park The best hotels, lodges, and cabins for a trip to the Last Frontier. By Bailey Berg October 25, 2026 Sheldon Chalet Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story With broad river valleys, colorful meadows peppered with fireweed and lupine, forests thick with spruce and aspen, and the snow-covered Alaska Range rising in the distance, Denali National Park and Preserve is one of those places that can still feel startlingly wild no matter how many times you visit. At 6.1 million acres, it’s larger than Massachusetts , and the sheer scale of the national park means a trip here can look very different depending on where you choose to stay. I lived in Alaska full-time for eight years (and now split my time between Alaska and Colorado ) and have been to Denali often. Over time, I got to know the best places travelers can base themselves in and around the park. The challenge of planning a trip to Denali isn’t necessarily finding somewhere to stay, but figuring out which part of the vast region makes the most sense as a home base for what you want to see. The cluster of lodges just outside the entrance, where restaurants, outfitters, and bus departures are all close at hand, is one of the go-to spots for first-time visitors. Nearby Healy and the long stretches of the Parks Highway offer more breathing room, with cabins, vacation rentals, and quieter stays scattered north and south of the park. And for travelers who want to go much deeper, Kantishna sits nearly 90 miles down Denali Park Road, offering a handful of remote lodges and the rare chance to stay deep inside the national park itself. I’ve selected the best stays across that spectrum, from full-service hotels and family-friendly cabins to secluded backcountry lodges and even a chalet set on a glacier just miles from the summit of North America’s highest peak. Read on for my favorite places to stay near Denali National Park in Alaska.
